source: Salge, Glackin, Polani (2014) Empowerment: an introduction
finding: Empowerment is the channel capacity from an agent's actuators to its sensors. Klyubin, Polani and Nehaniv introduced it in 2005. It measures how many different futures the agent can reliably cause.
numbers: Computed with Blahut-Arimoto. In a deterministic discrete world it equals the log of the number of states reachable in n steps.
quote: Empowerment is the channel capacity from an agent's actuators to its sensors
limits: Needs a model of the world and a choice of actuator and sensor variables. The value depends on that choice.
agent_relevance: For S7: a probe is good if it has many distinguishable outcomes, so the answer can change the next step.

source: Salge, Glackin, Polani (2014) Empowerment: an introduction (maze, section 4.5.1)
finding: The first empowerment demo, from Klyubin 2005a: a 10x10 maze with 5 actions (4 moves and stay). The agent looks 5 steps ahead. Cells that reach the most positions score highest, so the agent finds open areas and junctions with no goal.
numbers: 5-step empowerment in the 10x10 maze ranged from 3.46 to 5.52 bits. 5^5 = 3125 action sequences per cell.
limits: Toy deterministic grid. Action sequences grow as 5^n.
agent_relevance: Empowerment prefers states that keep options open, not states that satisfy a task.

source: Salge, Glackin, Polani (2014) Empowerment: an introduction (Anthony et al. 2008 centrality result)
finding: Anthony et al. (2008) found that local n-step empowerment correlates with a global graph property, closeness centrality, in box-pushing grids and scale-free random graphs. So a local option count carries global structure.
numbers: Reported as a 'strong indication'; the review gives no coefficient.
quote: these results show a strong indication of certain global aspects of various worlds being `coded' at a local level
limits: Breaks down when the horizon does not reach the box. Salge says it is unknown how general this is and suspects uneven worlds (pockets with different rules) will break it.
agent_relevance: Local probing reveals global structure only if the probe reaches it. Too short a reach misses it.

source: Salge, Glackin, Polani (2014) Empowerment: an introduction (sensor evolution, Klyubin 2005b/2008)
finding: A genetic algorithm evolved sensor layouts to maximise 4-step empowerment in an infinite grid with a marker gradient. Different start positions gave different layouts. Some spots had one good solution, others several near-equal ones. A small cost per sensor prevented degenerate layouts.
numbers: Five actions, n sensors; sensor value = which sensor sees the highest marker. Exact values are in figures only.
limits: Toy world. Needs a cost term to avoid piling on sensors.
agent_relevance: Supports choosing what to observe by information content, with a cost per probe.

source: Salge, Glackin, Polani (2014) Empowerment: an introduction (limits: flat landscape)
finding: If the horizon is long or the sensors are very rich, the agent can reach or tell apart everything, and empowerment is flat. Meaningful structure needs limited sensing and acting (the 'Tragedy of the Greek Gods').
numbers: A 100-step horizon gives log(100) everywhere in the example.
quote: all-knowing, all-powerful agents see no salient structure in the world
limits: Horizon and sensor resolution are free choices that decide the result.
agent_relevance: Do not over-extend lookahead. A probe that distinguishes everything tells nothing about which to pick.

source: Salge, Glackin, Polani (2014) Empowerment: an introduction (contraindication)
finding: Empowerment alone does not seek an externally set goal. If the goal state is not highly empowered, an empowerment-maximising agent will not go there.
numbers: No numbers. Stated as a clear contraindication.
quote: if an externally desired goal state is not highly empowered, then an empowerment-maximising algorithm is not going to seek it out
limits: Task-independent by design.
agent_relevance: Use empowerment or information gain only to choose probes, never to replace the task check (G3).

source: Salge, Glackin, Polani (2014) Empowerment: an introduction (pendulum, Jung et al. 2011 Monte Carlo)
finding: Jung et al. (2011) computed empowerment on a continuous pendulum by Monte Carlo sampling of action outcomes. A greedy controller sampled 5 actuation choices and took the one whose next state had highest expected empowerment. The pendulum swung up and balanced upright with no reward.
numbers: 5 candidate actions per step. Other time steps and power limits gave cycling or resting at the bottom.
limits: Result is not unique and depends on time step and power limit. Greedy choice can miss the best action between the samples.
agent_relevance: Sampling-based estimation of option count works without a closed-form model, which is how an LLM agent would have to do it.

source: Mohamed and Rezende (2015) Variational information maximisation for intrinsically motivated RL
finding: First scalable empowerment: a variational lower bound on mutual information, learned by a neural net that works from pixels. It removes the Blahut-Arimoto cost.
numbers: Blahut-Arimoto costs O(N K S^2) = O(N K D^4) for D x D grids and O(N K 2^(2D^2)) for binary images. In small rooms (<=400 states) the variational and exact landscapes matched (correlation 1.00, R2 0.90). Horizon K=5.
limits: Checked on small rooms and a 3D predator/prey toy. No external-task benchmark. The bound can be ill-posed in Gaussian models.
agent_relevance: The cost of exact option counting explodes with horizon. For an LLM agent, sample a few probes instead of enumerating.

source: Mohamed and Rezende (2015) experiments (dynamic worlds)
finding: Reproduced the Salge box-room result: empowerment is high near a movable box (a tool) and low near a fixed box. Agents also used keys, built walls against lava and fled a predator, each by picking the highest-empowerment next state.
numbers: One-step lookahead over 9 actions in the lava maze. Qualitative figures only.
limits: Demonstrations; no success-rate table and no baselines.
agent_relevance: Empowerment values things that can be changed. For an LLM, prefer probing parts of the problem that can be edited.

source: Gregor, Rezende, Wierstra (2016) Variational intrinsic control
finding: Learns options by maximising mutual information between a chosen option and the final state, given the start. Intrinsic reward is log q(option | start, end) minus log p(option). On average it equals the log of how many different end states the agent can reach.
numbers: Gridworlds, open and closed loop policies. In a 15x15 four-room world with reward at (3,3), agents pretrained without reward collected reward faster than pure REINFORCE (figure only).
limits: Hard to train: the intrinsic reward is noisy and moving. It failed with neural networks until they alternated fixing the reward and fixing the policy. A continuous option space made it harder; only some runs worked.
agent_relevance: Information-based motivation is unstable when the learner changes it. Keep probe scoring in fixed code (G5).

source: Gregor, Rezende, Wierstra (2016) Variational intrinsic control (MNIST control)
finding: On pairs of MNIST digits where 5 actions change digit classes, the agent learned to classify digits through control alone and reached nearly the maximum controllable states.
numbers: Empowerment 4.6 nats = exp(4.6) = 99.5 states with 10-action policies; maximum 100 controllable states out of 60000^2. Two random distractors did not change the empowerment reached in the four-room test.
limits: Single environment, one number.
agent_relevance: Empowerment ignores uncontrollable noise, the opposite of prediction-error curiosity.

source: Gregor, Rezende, Wierstra (2016) Variational intrinsic control (extrinsic transfer)
finding: After unsupervised option learning, intrinsic and extrinsic reward combined with a large weight (30) let the agent learn a new reward faster.
numbers: 15x15 four-room world, reward placed at (3,3). Figure only.
limits: Proof of principle on one gridworld.
agent_relevance: Task-free probing can pay off later, but gains are shown only on a toy.

source: Eysenbach et al. (2018) Diversity is all you need (DIAYN)
finding: DIAYN learns skills that reach states a discriminator can tell apart. Reward is log q(z|s) - log p(z), plus a policy entropy term. This is a mutual-information objective close to empowerment, with a fixed skill prior.
numbers: Soft actor-critic with entropy weight 0.1. Skills learned with no reward in half-cheetah, hopper and ant. Fine-tuning the best skill sped up learning on all three versus random initialisation.
limits: Pretraining cost is left out of the curves by assumption. The best skill is picked using the true reward.
agent_relevance: Diverse, distinguishable probes beat a few good ones when the task is unknown.

source: Eysenbach et al. (2018) Diversity is all you need (DIAYN) (versus VIC)
finding: DIAYN reports a failure of VIC: because VIC learns its skill prior, it sampled only a handful of skills (the 'Matthew effect'). DIAYN fixes a uniform prior so all skills keep training.
numbers: Effective number of skills exp(H[Z]) in half-cheetah: VIC collapsed to a handful, DIAYN stayed high (figure).
limits: One environment, authors' own comparison.
agent_relevance: Keep a uniform floor over probe types, or the few best-scoring ones take everything.

source: Houthooft et al. (2016) VIME
finding: Curiosity as information gain about dynamics. The bonus is the KL divergence between the Bayesian neural net posterior over dynamics before and after a transition, added to the reward. Used with TRPO, REINFORCE and ERWR.
numbers: Tasks: MountainCar, CartPoleSwingup, HalfCheetah (sparse reward +1), DoublePendulum, Walker2D, SwimmerGather. Dynamics net: 1 hidden layer of 32 units; batch 5000. Naive exploration and an L2 prediction-error bonus almost never reached the goal.
quote: VIME performs much better, achieving the goal in most cases
limits: Results are curves with no table. On CartPole better exploration was redundant. Adding Gaussian noise to rewards did not help. A bonus weight that is too high prioritises exploration over reward.
agent_relevance: Information gain helps when the signal is sparse and is wasted when greedy already solves it. Probe only when a check fails (G1).

source: Burda et al. (2018) Random network distillation
finding: A competing intrinsic reward, prediction error against a fixed random network. The paper states that forward-prediction-error methods suffer from the 'noisy TV' problem in stochastic settings.
numbers: A results row of 3,906 / 8,152 / -3 / 8,666 / 3,282 / 1,859 appears in the paper's hard-exploration Atari table; which row label it is was not checked.
limits: Atari scores come from this paper only; the empowerment papers did not run Atari.
agent_relevance: Choose probes by what the answer could change, not by how surprising the answer is.

source: Hafner, Ortega, Ba, Parr, Friston, Heess (2022) Action and perception as divergence minimization
finding: One objective, the KL divergence between actual and target distributions over inputs and latents, yields many agents. Different targets give maximum-entropy RL, empowerment, information gain, skill discovery and active inference. Realized empowerment is mutual information between actions and future inputs; the paper generalises it to all future inputs.
numbers: Theory paper. Its table maps actions to empowerment (VIM, ACIE, EPC) and parameters to information gain (VIME, MAX, Plan2Explore).
limits: No new experiments in the main text. Unification is by derivation.
agent_relevance: Information gain and empowerment are two ends of one family: learn about the world versus control it. Probe choice can use either.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2020) Whence the expected free energy?
finding: Active inference picks policies by expected free energy (EFE), which splits into extrinsic value and epistemic value (expected information gain). The paper shows the EFE is not simply the free energy extended into the future.
numbers: The 'free energy of the future' has an epistemic term with the opposite sign, so it would discourage information seeking.
quote: the FEF actively discourages information-seeking behaviour
limits: Theory. The paper traces the epistemic term to a prior belief that the agent will reach its preferred outcomes, which is a modelling choice.
agent_relevance: Exploration is not free in this theory. The info-seeking term is a design choice, which fits adding it only by explicit code.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Compares active inference with RL. Reward is just another observation with a preference over it. With zero prior preference over reward, agents still explore through epistemic value. One objective balances exploration and exploitation without a temperature setting.
numbers: Qualitative comparison with bandit and maze examples. No benchmark table.
limits: Authors are active-inference proponents; small tasks.
agent_relevance: Gives the risk versus ambiguity vocabulary for asking whether a probe resolves a real doubt.

source: Tschantz, Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2020) Reinforcement learning through active inference
finding: A deep active inference agent with an ensemble model and information gain over transition parameters. It solved MountainCar in one trial where reward-only and variance-seeking baselines did not, and ran in a reward-free Ant maze.
numbers: MountainCar: 25 episodes of at most 200 steps, optimal in a single trial. Cup Catch: comparable to baselines. Cheetah Run and Flip compared with SAC after 100 episodes; Ant Maze coverage versus random.
limits: Workshop paper; figures not tables. Cup Catch showed no benefit, which the authors attribute to easy reward.
agent_relevance: Sparse-signal tasks benefit from information gain; easy ones do not.

source: Tschantz et al. (2020) Scaling active inference
finding: Scales active inference to continuous control. Downloaded but only the title was checked; no findings are claimed.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Open in a later pass.

source: Bialek, Nemenman, Tishby (2001) Predictability, complexity and learning
finding: Defines predictive information I_pred(T), the mutual information between a past segment and the future. It is finite, grows as log T, or grows as a power law. For a model with a finite number of parameters it grows as log T, with a coefficient that counts the model dimension.
numbers: Log growth for finite-parameter models; power law for nonparametric models. The exact coefficient was not checked in the text.
limits: Needs a stationary process. No agent experiment.
agent_relevance: Predictive information is the formal base of 'probe what teaches the most about the future'.

source: Still and Precup (2012) An information-theoretic approach to curiosity-driven RL
finding: Not opened. Known from citations only: curiosity derived from maximising predictive information.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Listed for a later pass.

source: Lindley (1956) expected information gain, as formulated in BED-LLM
finding: The classical formula: EIG(x) = H[p(theta)] - E[H[p(theta|y;x)]], the mutual information between a hypothesis and an answer. VIME and empowerment maximise related quantities.
numbers: Equation 1 of the BED-LLM paper (opened). Lindley's own paper was not opened.
limits: Needs a model of the answerer.
agent_relevance: The cleanest formula for S7: pick the probe with the highest expected drop in hypothesis entropy.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts (UoT)
finding: An LLM planner simulates answers to candidate questions, scores each by information gain over the set of possibilities, and propagates reward over a short tree. Tested on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis (DX, MedDG) and troubleshooting (FloDial).
numbers: Average success rate +38.1% (relative) over direct prompting across five datasets and several LLMs. GPT-4 troubleshooting 43.7% to 67.3%; DX 97.0% (GPT-4, closed set). Uncertainty reward added 5.9% to ToT on average. Simulation depth limited to three steps.
limits: Answerer is simulated by GPT-4 (checked on 10% of dialogues). Information gain uses the model's own guesses of the possibility set. Gains are relative percent.
agent_relevance: The nearest LLM test of S7: score probes by expected information gain in code, then pick.

source: Li et al. (2023) Eliciting human preferences with language models (GATE)
finding: LMs ask open-ended questions or generate edge cases to learn a person's preferences. Pre-registered study, 388 participants, three domains: email validation, content recommendation, moral reasoning.
numbers: Area under the p(correct)-vs-time curve was higher for GATE than for supervised learning, pool-based active learning or user-written prompts, with significance only in content recommendation and email validation. Mean entropy of per-question yes-probability across people: 0.77 bits.
limits: Not significant in moral reasoning. Questions come from prompting, not an explicit information-gain computation.
agent_relevance: Asking is less effort for people than writing a prompt, but the gain depends on domain.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM
finding: Chooses LLM questions by expected information gain computed from the LLM's own predictive distribution over answers, with hypotheses sampled and filtered for consistency with the history. Beats prompt-only and a split baseline in 20 Questions.
numbers: Mean +37.4 percentage points over direct prompting. 20 Questions final success across GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Llama-3.3-70B, Mistral-Large, Qwen2.5-72B: Animals 90 to 100%, Celebrities 70 to 100%, Things 60 to 80% (read from figure). Preference task: 200 users, 10 film ratings.
limits: Gains in preference elicitation were smaller because prompt-only is a stronger baseline there. Benefit held when answerer was a different model.
agent_relevance: Ablations: in-context belief updating gave massive drops; asking the LLM to pick the highest-EIG question worked much less well than computing it. This supports G5 (code selects).

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM (marginal entropy is not EIG)
finding: With a deterministic answer model, EIG collapses to the entropy of the predicted answer. When answers are noisy, a question with high entropy but also high conditional entropy is a poor probe.
numbers: Figure 1 contrasts two questions with equal marginal entropy and different EIG. The Entropy ablation scored below full EIG.
limits: Needs several LLM calls per candidate question.
agent_relevance: Rank probes by information gain, not by how uncertain the answer is.
